data.claim: A failed import of a lazily re-exported submodule poisons sys.modules[<pkg>.<sub>] = None, and importlib.import_module then re-raises ModuleNotFoundError on every later access WITHOUT re-importing, so _reexport.__getattr__ must drop the poison before retrying
data.falsifier: Import a throwaway package, poison sys.modules[pkg.sub]=None, install _reexport and access a lazy name: it resolves (no ModuleNotFoundError)
data.mechanism: importlib sets sys.modules[fullname]=None on a failed import; a subsequent import_module(fullname) sees the None and raises ModuleNotFoundError without re-executing the module, so a transient submodule failure (ddflow.services.ci.main) becomes permanent within the process
data.probe_output: ModuleNotFoundError: import of demo_probe.sub halted; None in sys.modules
data.question: Why does check_after_merge crash with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'ddflow.services.ci.main' via ddflow.core._reexport.__getattr__ on every merge, and what must the lazy re-export do?

evidence.note: Confirmed: importlib poisons sys.modules[fullname]=None on a failed submodule import; a later importlib.import_module re-raises ModuleNotFoundError without re-importing (probe output: 'import of demo_probe.sub halted; None in sys.modules'). The fix drops the poison before retry; probe: first access fails (poison set), second access resolves to 7. Research Recbc02c9db.

ddflow brief --item fix-B7e585f9e5d: read r-gemini-key-load (export GEMINI_API_KEY before gemini review) and r-task-phase-needs-wave (bug fix task carries wave tag via bugs-2 parent). Change is a 10-line fix to ddflow/core/_reexport.py + a new regression test; no external dependency, no new knob, no layering change.

Worktree ddflow/fix-B7e585f9e5d commit 1c6659c2b: (1) ddflow/core/_reexport.py __getattr__ drops a poisoned sys.modules[fullname]=None before import_module retry so a transient submodule-import failure self-heals; (2) tests/test_regression_reexport_self_heal.py pins it. Probe before fix: first access fails, poison set, second access STILL re-raises ModuleNotFoundError; after fix: second access resolves to 7.

chunk_findings.detail: The regression test never builds the `sys.modules[name] is None` poison the new branch deletes, so it passes on the unfixed `__getattr__`. Unlinking `poisondep.py` makes `poisonpkg/sub.py` load and then fail inside `exec_module`; importlib's failure path removes `sys.modules["poisonpkg.sub"]` rather than storing `None`. `sys.modules.get("poisonpkg.sub") is None` is true for a missing key as well, so the assertion does not prove a poison entry. Restoring `poisondep.py` and reading `poisonpkg.MAGIC` therefore succeeds without the `del sys.modules[fullname]` lines, and the test does not fail on the pre-fix code or exercise the B7e585f9e5d retry.

data.probe: Confirmed: the first test was vacuous -- modern CPython DELETES a failed module from sys.modules (del sys.modules[spec.name] on exec failure, _bootstrap.py:936-941), so the retry recovered without the fix. Rewrote the test to set the 'None in sys.modules' sentinel directly: unfixed __getattr__ re-raises ModuleNotFoundError, fixed __getattr__ drops the sentinel and re-imports -> MAGIC==7 (verified both trees).

chunk_findings.detail: The None-sentinel cleanup is a non-atomic check-then-delete. Thread A can observe `sys.modules[fullname] is None`, then be preempted; thread B can finish `import_module` and store the live module; thread A then executes `del sys.modules[fullname]` and removes that live module. The next importer in the same process raises `ModuleNotFoundError` for a module that had already loaded, which is the failure this change claims to stop.

chunk_findings.detail: `import poisonpkg` and `sys.modules["poisonpkg.sub"] = None` are not undone (`monkeypatch` only restores `sys.path`). After the test, `tmp_path` is deleted while `sys.modules["poisonpkg"]` still points at it. A later `import poisonpkg` / `import poisonpkg.sub` in the same process uses that stale entry and raises `ModuleNotFoundError` or `ImportError` against a directory that no longer exists.

chunk_findings.detail: The new `RLock` is held across `importlib.import_module`, which runs arbitrary module body code while the import machinery holds that module's lock. Interleaving: thread T1 enters this `__getattr__`, takes `lock`, and starts `import_module(f"{package}.{sub}")`, which then blocks on another module M still being initialized; thread T2 is inside M's body and touches any lazy name on the same package, so it waits for `lock`. T1 waits on M's import lock and T2 waits on `lock`, and both hang. Before this change there was no lock to invert with the import lock; `RLock` only covers same-thread reentry, not this cross-thread order.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/core/_reexport.py:55

data.probe: Confirmed: the RLock held across import_module can invert with importlib's per-module lock (T1 holds the reexport lock and blocks on module M; T2 inside M's body touches a lazy name and waits on the reexport lock). Removed the lock entirely: the fix is now a split drop-sentinel-then-import with no held lock across importlib.import_module.

chunk_findings.detail: `if sys.modules.get(fullname) is None: sys.modules.pop(fullname, None)` treats a missing key the same as a halt sentinel, and the pop is not atomic with the following `import_module` now that the package lock is gone. Two threads resolving the same lazy name before the submodule is in `sys.modules` both see `get(...) is None`. T2 pops (no-op), `import_module` inserts the module and runs its body; T1 then `pop`s that live entry out from under T2 and imports a second copy. Module identity, registrations, and any body that expects `sys.modules[__name__]` break on ordinary concurrent first access, not only after a halted import. The old `in sys.modules and value is None` check inside the lock did not delete a module another thread had just installed.

data.probe: Confirmed: the pop-on-missing in the success path could delete another thread's live module. Moved the sentinel drop into an except ModuleNotFoundError retry-once: import_module gets first shot (its own lock serializes import), and the pop fires only AFTER it raised, where the entry is a halt sentinel (or absent), never a live module. A genuinely absent submodule re-raises on the retry.

chunk_findings.detail: `except ModuleNotFoundError` always calls `import_module` a second time, and `sys.modules.get(fullname) is None` is true both for the halt sentinel and for a missing key, so the retry is not limited to `fullname in sys.modules and sys.modules[fullname] is None`. Given a real submodule whose body appends to a registry and then raises `ModuleNotFoundError` (missing dependency, `.name` not equal to `fullname`), importlib clears the partial entry, this handler treats that as a sentinel, and the module body runs twice before the error escapes. The old path imported once. If that first execution installs the missing name, the retry succeeds and `cache[sub] = mod` hides the failure.

data.probe: Confirmed: unconditional second import_module would re-run a genuinely-broken submodule's body twice and could mask its failure. Retry is now gated on the halt-sentinel only (fullname in sys.modules and sys.modules[fullname] is None); a real import failure deletes the entry and re-raises without a second exec.
